title: Platform work is expanding opportunity while shifting income volatility, safety risk, and bargaining power onto workers
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Diagnostic review of working conditions and social security coverage of digital platform workers in Cambodia
geography: Phnom Penh, Cambodia, with national legal and platform-market context

workforce_scope.value: delivery riders, tuk-tuk drivers and taxi drivers using location-based digital labour platforms

qualitative_scope.value: 29 in-depth worker interviews and 10 key-informant interviews

work_intensity.value: workers averaged roughly 6.7–6.8 days per week and 11–12 hours per day including unpaid waiting time

observations.method: Mixed-method diagnostic combining a Phnom Penh worker survey, in-depth interviews, key-informant interviews, desk review and a tripartite consultation.
observations.uncertainty: The worker evidence is exploratory and geographically limited to Phnom Penh; it is not representative of Cambodia as a whole or a longitudinal estimate of platform-work growth.
observations.subgroup: Delivery riders, tuk-tuk drivers, taxi drivers, platform operators, government, unions and worker associations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Platform work can provide flexible income and access to employment, especially where stable alternatives are limited, even as long hours and unpaid waiting expose workers to insecurity.

observations.period: 2026 publication; platform earnings and operating-cost structure

denominator.unit: reported comparison across three worker categories

gross_monthly_earnings.value: taxi drivers US$581; delivery riders US$501; tuk-tuk drivers US$477
gross_monthly_earnings.unit: US dollars per month before operating expenses

net_position.value: taxi drivers had the highest gross earnings but retained the least after high operating costs; delivery riders retained more after expenses than the other categories

bargaining_pressure.value: workers reported financial instability from competition and limited power to negotiate trip fares and commission fees

observations.method: Survey estimates and qualitative findings analyzed by service type.
observations.uncertainty: Earnings and expense figures are study estimates for the sampled Phnom Penh workers and should not be treated as platform-wide income accounts or household disposable income.
observations.subgroup: Taxi drivers, delivery riders and tuk-tuk drivers operating under different vehicle and platform cost structures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher gross earnings or multi-platform access may still make platform work economically attractive relative to available alternatives, despite cost and fee pressure.

observations.period: 2026 publication; algorithmic management, safety and voice

ratings_control.value: a large majority reported that customer ratings significantly affect earnings and task allocation

penalties.value: nearly half reported penalties such as reduced job allocation or account suspension for refusing or cancelling orders

injury.value: one third of delivery riders reported having been injured while working

representation.value: informal worker networks exist but trade unionization is virtually absent

observations.method: Mixed-method analysis of automated systems, occupational safety and health, dispute resolution, social protection and worker organization.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported and study-specific findings; they establish a pattern of perceived algorithmic and institutional exposure, not a causal estimate of platform-system effects.
observations.subgroup: Workers subject to ratings, task allocation, penalties, account suspension, accident risk and limited collective bargaining.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ratings and automated allocation can coordinate demand and create access to work, while penalties may be intended as service-quality controls; the distribution of costs and appeal rights remains the central issue.

observations.period: 2026 publication; legal classification and social-protection boundary

denominator.unit: Cambodian platform-work legal and protection framework

classification.value: platforms mostly classify workers as independent contractors or partners rather than employees

coverage.value: voluntary NSSF healthcare can be available to self-employed workers, while pension and occupational-risk coverage are separate and not included in that voluntary healthcare scheme

policy_direction.value: the report calls for clearer employment classification, stronger social protection and occupational safety and health measures

observations.method: Review of Cambodian law and policy combined with worker, platform, government and worker-organization evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Legal coverage and implementation may change; this record captures the report’s 2026 description and does not independently adjudicate worker classification or legal compliance.
observations.subgroup: Independent contractors, platform workers, social-security institutions, regulators and platform operators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Independent status may preserve entry and scheduling flexibility, but without portable protections it can externalize accident, income, retirement and dispute-resolution risks.

related_sources.claim: Official DOI record for the ILO Cambodia platform-work diagnostic.

boundary: This record adds a platform-work signal linking digital convenience and employment access to unpaid waiting, operating costs, algorithmic management, injury exposure, legal classification, social protection and worker voice. It is a Phnom Penh diagnostic and not a national labor-market estimate, causal evaluation, or basis for generalizing all platform workers globally.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ILO publication page and downloadable report were reviewed for sample scope, work intensity, earnings and expenses, algorithmic management, injuries, representation, legal classification and social-protection findings.
